question:
A risk consultant is advising a small Australian mutual bank that used the TSA under Basel II and has now moved to the SA. The bank has ten years of high-quality loss data, including several large fraud losses, and its supervisor has not exercised national discretion to include internal loss data for banks in the first BI bucket. The bank’s figures, converted to EUR, are shown below.

| Item (EUR-equivalent) | Amount (EUR million) |
|---|---|
| Business indicator, three-year average | 750 |
| Gross income, three-year average | 680 |
| Average annual operational losses, past ten years | 30 |

The bank’s minimum operational risk capital under the SA is closest to:

options.C: EUR 112.5 million
options.D: EUR 150.8 million

solution:
Stem summary: Small Australian bank, BI EUR 750 million, large loss history; SA capital.

**Concept and theory**

The SA applies the ILM only to banks above the first bucket. GARP 24.2: “For banks in bucket 1 (ie with BI ≤ EUR 1 billion), internal loss data does not affect the capital calculation. question: A junior analyst at a UK bank notes that the percentages 12%, 15% and 18% appear both in the Basel II standardized approach (TSA) and in the Basel III SA, and asks a senior analyst whether the two approaches use them in the same way. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.A: Both the TSA and the SA set 12%, 15% and 18% by the perceived riskiness of each business line; the SA only swaps gross income for the business indicator as the exposure proxy.
options.B: The TSA set 12%, 15% and 18% by business line, whereas the SA sets them by BI size, with the coefficient of a bank’s bucket applied to its whole BI once the bank enters that bucket.
options.C: The TSA set 12%, 15% and 18% by the size of a bank’s gross income, whereas the SA sets them by business line, using the business indicator rather than gross income as the exposure proxy.
options.D: The TSA set 12%, 15% and 18% by business line, whereas the SA applies them as marginal coefficients to successive slices of the BI, so that capital grows more than proportionally with size.

solution:
Stem summary: UK analyst asks whether 12%, 15% and 18% mean the same in the TSA and the SA.

**Concept and theory**

The same three percentages appear in both regimes, which makes them a classic trap.

**TSA (Basel II).** Gross income was split into eight business lines. Each line’s income was multiplied by a beta of 12%, 15% or 18% “depending on the perceived riskiness of the underlying business line” (GARP Chapter 2). For example, retail banking was weighted 12% and trading and sales 18%.

**SA (Basel III).** The exposure proxy is the business indicator, which “replaces the ‘gross income’ used in the former TSA approach.” The percentages are now marginal coefficients by size: 12% on BI up to EUR 1 billion, 15% on BI from EUR 1 billion to 30 billion, and 18% on BI above EUR 30 billion. question: A regulator at a national supervisory authority is comparing the supervisory work required under the AMA with that required under the SA. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: Under the AMA, the supervisor prescribed one loss distribution model for all banks; under the SA, the supervisor must validate each bank’s own internal capital model before it can be used.
options.B: Under the AMA, approval typically took about three years and needed independent validation; under the SA, a bank that fails the loss data standards may return to its approved AMA model.
options.C: Under the AMA, the supervisor validated each bank’s own model, which took about three years to prepare; under the SA, a bank that fails the loss data standards holds at least 100% of the BIC.
options.D: Under the AMA, approval typically took about three years and needed independent validation; under the SA, if the supervisor sets the ILM to one, banks need not disclose historical losses.

solution:
Stem summary: Regulator comparing supervisory work under the AMA and the SA.

**Concept and theory**

**AMA.** Banks were “free to assess their own capital needs, provided that the regulatory authority of each country . . . validates its model and framework” (GARP Chapter 2). question: A senior risk analyst at a bank that used the AMA until the SA took effect is advising the head of operational risk. options.A: Like any bank with fewer than ten years of data, it is expected to use the five-year transitional treatment, and it may keep its AMA model for Pillar 1 capital until ten years of data exist.
options.B: The five-year transitional treatment is not expected to apply to banks that used the AMA, and the modeling team’s expertise can be redeployed to Pillar 2 capital assessment and stress testing.
options.C: Because it has fewer than ten years of high-quality data, it must calculate its capital requirement based solely on the BIC, and the modeling team’s expertise is no longer of any regulatory use.
options.D: The five-year transitional treatment is mandatory for banks that used the AMA, and the output of the bank’s former AMA model acts as a floor on its SA operational risk capital requirement.

solution:
Stem summary: Former AMA bank with six years of loss data and a large modeling team.

**Concept and theory**

**Data window and transition.** The LC must be based on ten years of high-quality annual loss data. As part of the transition, banks without ten years “may use a minimum of five years”; banks without five years must calculate capital solely on the BIC (GARP 24.2). question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on the general criteria for internally generated loss data used in the loss component of the Basel III standardised approach for operational risk. The bank is about to move to the standardised approach for the first time. Which of the following statements about the observation period should she present as most accurate?

options.A: A five-year observation period is the standard requirement, and it is extended to ten years once the bank has built up ten years of high-quality loss data.
options.B: A ten-year observation period is required; five years is accepted exceptionally on first adoption if good-quality data are unavailable beyond five years.
options.C: A ten-year observation period is required, but any bank may move to five years at any time if its supervisor judges its older loss data to be of poor quality.

Stem summary: Canadian bank analyst presenting the loss data observation period to new hires, bank about to adopt the standardised approach.

**Concept and theory**

Under the Basel III standardised approach, a bank’s own loss history enters capital through the loss component (LC), which is built from average annual operational risk losses. An average is only meaningful if it covers enough years to capture the rare, severe events that dominate operational risk: a short window can easily contain no large loss at all, or one freak year, and either way it would misstate the bank’s exposure. That is why the Basel Committee fixes the length of the window as the first general criterion for loss data.

question:

question: The chief risk officer of a Brazilian banking group is briefing the board risk committee on loss collection thresholds under the Basel III standardised approach. The group’s business indicator is equivalent to about €14 billion. A committee member asks how the threshold for including loss events works. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.A: The minimum threshold is €20,000; at national discretion, supervisors may raise it to €100,000 for average annual losses, for banks with a BI above €1 billion.
options.B: The minimum threshold is €20,000; the bank itself may raise it to €100,000 after its first year on the standardised approach, with no supervisory role.
options.C: The minimum threshold is €20,000; at national discretion, supervisors may raise it to €100,000 for every bank, bucket 1 banks using loss data included.
options.D: The minimum threshold is €100,000; at national discretion, supervisors may lower it to €20,000 for average annual losses, for banks with a BI above €1 billion.

solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian group CRO (BI about EUR 14 billion) explaining the loss collection threshold to the board risk committee.

**Concept and theory**

A loss data set must be comprehensive: GARP 24.5(d) requires internal loss data to capture all material activities and exposures from all appropriate subsystems and geographic locations. Comprehensiveness, however, does not mean recording every trivial error. A minimum threshold separates events that must be captured from immaterial noise and keeps the average annual loss comparable across banks.

options.A: Descriptive information on the drivers or causes of each loss event must be collected, with a level of detail commensurate with the size of the gross loss.

question:

|---|---|---|
| E1 | Forged collateral documents on a mortgage; the loss is accounted for in credit risk RWAs as a defaulted exposure | 1,850 |

question: A risk consultant is advising a Singapore bank on how recoveries should be treated when it builds its SGD loss data set under the Basel III standardised approach. The bank’s draft policy contains four candidate statements. Which of the following statements should the consultant endorse as most accurate?

options.A: Reductions in corporate income tax liability caused by an operational loss count as recoveries and may be used to reduce the loss in the data set.
options.B: Only non-insurance recoveries may reduce a loss; insurance recoveries stay in the loss so that the data show losses before any risk transfer.
options.C: Once an insurer confirms a claim in writing, the receivable counts as a recovery and may reduce the loss before any payment is received.

GARP 24.6 defines three amounts that every loss event must support:

- **Gross loss**: the loss before recoveries of any type.
- **Net loss**: the loss after taking into account the impact of recoveries.
- **Recovery**: an independent occurrence, related to the original loss event, separate in time, in which funds or inflows of economic benefits are received from a third party. Examples: payments from insurers, repayments from perpetrators of fraud, recoveries of misdirected transfers.

question:

question:
A senior risk analyst at a Chinese commercial bank is reviewing two CNY items for the bank’s standardised approach loss data set.

- A material failed payment of CNY 12 million has a definitive financial impact, but it is still booked in a suspense account and is not yet reflected in the P&L.
- A material booking error overstated revenue across two prior financial accounting periods and was corrected this year with a negative adjustment of CNY 30 million. The error has given rise to no legal risk.

Which of the following best describes how the Basel Committee’s specific criteria treat these items?

options.A: Both are required: the failed payment because its impact is definitive, and the booking error because it is material and spans more than one period.
options.B: Neither is required: the failed payment because it is not yet in the P&L, and the booking error because its net impact over time is zero.
options.C: Only the booking error is required, as it has been booked in the P&L, while the failed payment enters only once it leaves the suspense account.
options.D: Only the failed payment is required, within a period commensurate with its size and age; the booking error is not, as it creates no legal risk.

Two of GARP’s gross loss inclusions deal with losses whose accounting is out of step with the economics.

question:
A compliance officer at a UK bank is recording a GBP mis-selling case in the bank’s loss database. The timeline of the case is shown below.

| Step | Date |
|---|---|
| Overcharging of customers begins | 14 February 2021 |
| Internal audit identifies the overcharging | 9 November 2022 |
| Customers file a legal claim against the bank | 14 March 2023 |
| Legal reserve for the probable estimated loss established in the P&L | 30 June 2024 |
| Settlement paid to customers | 12 May 2025 |

Under the Basel Committee’s specific criteria, what is the latest reference date the bank may use to include this legal loss in its loss data set?

options.C: 14 March 2023
options.D: 9 November 2022

solution:
Stem summary: UK bank compliance officer choosing the latest reference date for a legal mis-selling loss from a five-step timeline.

**Concept and theory**

A loss event has several dates (occurrence, discovery, accounting), and the loss data set must pick one to decide which year a loss falls into. GARP 24.6 sets the rules:

- Banks must use the **date of accounting** for building the loss data set.
- For legal events, the bank must use a date **no later than the date of accounting**.
- For legal loss events, the date of accounting is the date when a **legal reserve is established** **for the probable estimated loss in the P&L**.

loText: Describe the evolution of the stress testing process and compare the methodologies of historical European Banking Association (EBA), Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), and Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) stress tests.
question:
A risk consultant is presenting on the evolution of macro-prudential stress testing requirements established in response to the global financial crisis of 2007 – 2009. The consultant compares features of the following three stress tests:

- The 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) test
- The 2011 European Banking Association (EBA) test
- The 2012 Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) test

Which of the following elements of these stress tests or their resulting impacts is correct for the analyst to include in the presentation?

options.A: Several Spanish banks failed the EBA stress test, and Spain imposed stricter countrywide stress tests the following year that resulted in some banks raising capital.
options.B: The SCAP stress test scenario was less severe compared to later US stress tests and did not result in any increased capital requirements for participating banks.
options.C: The CCAR test required banks to evaluate both a base case and a stress scenario, while the EBA test only included a stress scenario.
options.D: The SCAP test only disclosed overall loss rates for retail and commercial exposures, while the EBA test expanded disclosure to individual geographical regions and asset classes.

solution:
**Concept**

Evolution of stress tests. SCAP (US, 2009): a single stress scenario, with bank-level results by asset class published; ten banks had to raise USD 75 billion. CCAR (US, from 2011): annual, linked to capital plans. EBA (Europe, 2011): base and stress scenarios, with detailed disclosure, followed by further tests in Spain.

**Exam trap.** Each wrong option swaps a feature between the three exercises. SCAP did lead to capital raising and did disclose loss rates by asset class.

Family Bank has entered a \$100 million interest rate swap with a corporation. The swap has a remaining maturity of five years. The current value of the swap is \$4.5 million. The table below gives add-on factors as a percentage of principal for derivatives.

| Time remaining to maturity | Interest rate | Equity |
|---|---|---|
| \< 1 year | 0.0 | 6.0 |
| 1 to 5 years | 0.5 | 8.0 |
| > 5 years | 1.5 | 10.0 |

Based on the table above, the equivalent risk-weighted asset (RWA) under Basel I is closest to:
solution:
**Concept**

Basel I converts a derivative into a credit equivalent amount: current exposure plus an add-on, max$(V, 0) + a \times L$, where $a$ is the add-on factor and $L$ the principal. The credit equivalent amount is then multiplied by the counterparty’s risk weight. For a corporate counterparty the risk weight on derivatives is 50%.

**Working**

**Add-on:** interest rate contract with 1 to 5 years remaining, factor 0.5%: 0.005 × 100 = \$0.5 million **Credit equivalent amount:** 4.5 + 0.5 = \$5.0 million

**Risk-weighted assets:** 0.50 × 5.0 = \$2.5 million

**Exam trap.** Two steps: credit equivalent amount, then risk weight. Stopping after the first gives option A. A maturity of exactly five years falls in the 1-to-5-year bucket, not the over-5-year bucket.

loText: Explain the calculation of risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement per the original Basel I guidelines.
question:
XYZ bank has the following figures on its balance sheet:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Common stock | \$1.2 billion |
| Unrealized long-term marketable equity securities gain | \$10 million |
| Allowance in anticipation of possible credit losses | \$10 million |
| Goodwill | \$60 million |

Based solely on this information, the Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital numbers are, respectively:

options.C: \$1.22 billion, \$90 million
options.D: \$1.2 billion, \$80 million

solution:
**Concept**

Under the original Basel capital definitions, Tier 1 (core) capital is common equity and disclosed reserves, less goodwill. Tier 2 (supplementary) capital includes revaluation reserves, general loan loss reserves and subordinated debt.

**Working**

**Tier 1:** $1{,}200 - 60 = \$1{,}140 \text{million} = \$1.14$ billion

**Tier 2:** revaluation reserve 10 + loan loss allowance 10 = \$20 million

**Exam trap.** Goodwill is deducted from Tier 1; it is never added anywhere. Revaluation gains and loan loss reserves are Tier 2 items.

loText: Describe measures introduced in the 1995 and 1996 amendments, including guidelines for netting of credit exposures and methods for calculating market risk capital for assets in the trading book.
question: Pillar 1 of the Basel II framework allows banks to use a host of approaches to compute capital requirements for operational risk, credit risk, and market risk. Which of the following Basel II approaches allows a bank to explicitly recognize diversification benefits?

options.A: The Foundation Internal Ratings Based (IRB) Approach for credit risk
options.B: The Advanced IRB Approach for credit risk
options.C: The Standardized Approach for operational risk
options.D: The Internal Models Approach for market risk

solution:
**Concept**

The 1996 Amendment let banks use an internal models approach for market risk, based on their own VaR models. Because VaR is computed on the whole trading portfolio with empirical correlations, diversification is recognised explicitly. The credit risk IRB approaches use a supervisory formula with prescribed correlations.

**Exam trap.** “Internal” does not mean “free to model correlation”. Under IRB the bank supplies inputs to a formula it cannot change.

loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
question:
A German bank has chosen to use the standardized approach to calculate its capital charge for operational risk. Its annual gross revenue is distributed across only three business lines — Corporate Finance, Retail Banking, and Trading and Sales. The stated distribution of annual gross revenues (in \$ million) is as follows:

| Business line | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 | Beta factor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corporate Finance | 40 | 40 | 30 | 20% |
| Retail Banking | 20 | 15 | −50 | 18% |
| Trading and Sales | 20 | 10 | 10 | 15% |

The bank’s capital requirement for operational risk is closest to:
solution:
**Concept**

Basel II standardized approach for operational risk: each business line’s gross income is multiplied by its own beta factor. A negative amount in one business line can offset positive amounts in the same year. A year whose total is negative is ignored when averaging, as the reading’s worked example shows.

**Working**

|  | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Corporate Finance (20%) | 40 × 0.20 = 8.0 | 40 × 0.20 = 8.0 | 30 × 0.20 = 6.0 |
| Retail Banking (18%) | 20 × 0.18 = 3.6 | 15 × 0.18 = 2.7 | −50 × 0.18 = −9.0 |
| Trading and Sales (15%) | 20 × 0.15 = 3.0 | 10 × 0.15 = 1.5 | 10 × 0.15 = 1.5 |
| Total | 14.6 | 12.2 | −1.5 |

Year 3 has a negative total and is ignored.

Capital $= \frac{14.6 + 12.2}{2} = \$13.4$ million

**Exam trap.** Offsetting happens within a […]

loText: Compare the basic indicator approach, the standardized approach, and the advanced measurement approach for the calculation of operational risk capital under Basel II.
question: Which of the following statements about the methodologies for calculating an operational risk capital charge under Basel II is incorrect?

options.A: The basic indicator approach does not reflect the operational risk in a firm since it uses only revenue.
options.B: The standardized approach assumes that different business lines have different multipliers.
options.C: Under no circumstances does Basel II allow a national regulator to permit a bank to use an alternative standardized approach.
options.D: Advanced measurement approaches allow an institution to adopt its own method of assessment of operational risk.

solution:
**Concept**

Three Basel II approaches to operational risk capital. Basic indicator: 15% of average annual gross income. Standardized: gross income by business line, each with its own multiplier. Advanced measurement: the bank’s own internal model of the 99.9th percentile loss.

**Exam trap.** The question asks for the incorrect statement. Three true statements and one absolute claim: the absolute claim is the one to test.

**Answer-key note.** The alternative standardized approach is not described in the 2026 reading. The answer can be reached by elimination, since statements A, B and D all follow directly from the reading.

loText: Summarize elements of the Solvency II capital framework for insurance companies.
question: Pillar 1 of Solvency II specifies a minimum capital requirement (MCR) and a solvency capital requirement (SCR). Under the internal models approach of calculating SCR, the internal model used must satisfy several tests, except:

options.C: Validity test
options.D: Statistical quality test

solution:
**Concept**

Solvency II for insurers has three pillars like Basel II. Pillar 1 sets a minimum capital requirement (MCR) and a solvency capital requirement (SCR). The SCR can be calculated with a standardized approach or with an internal model, and an internal model must meet three criteria: sound data and methodology (statistical quality), calibration to the regulator’s target (calibration), and genuine use in business decisions (use test).

**Exam trap.** An “except” question. Three real names and one plausible invention. Learn the three as a set: statistical quality, calibration, use.

loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
question:
A bank is using the VaR and stressed VaR market risk framework in line with the Basel II.5 guidelines. The bank’s internal models for market risk have generated the following risk measures (in USD million) for the current trading book positions:

| Confidence level | Latest available 10-day VaR | Latest available 10-day stressed VaR | Average 10-day VaR of previous 60 days | Average 10-day stressed VaR of previous 60 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 95.0% | 238 | 484 | 252 | 546 |
| 99.0% | 451 | 995 | 413 | 1,106 |
| 99.9% | 578 | 1,281 | 528 | 1,372 |

Assuming the supervisory authority has set the multiplication factors for both the VaR and the stressed VaR values to 3, what is the correct capital requirement for general market risk for the bank under Basel II.5?

options.C: USD 4,557 million
options.D: USD 4,799 million

solution:
**Concept**

Basel 2.5 capital for general market risk: max$(\text{VaR}_{t-1}, m_{c} \text{VaR}_{\text{avg}}) + \text{max}(\text{sVaR}_{t-1}, m_{s} \text{sVaR}_{\text{avg}})$, with 10-day measures at the 99% confidence level.

**Working**

Use the 99.0% row: latest VaR 451, latest stressed VaR 995, average VaR 413, average stressed VaR 1,106.

**VaR term:** max$(451, 3 \times413) = \text{max}(451, 1{,}239) = 1{,}239$

**Stressed VaR term:** max$(995, 3 \times1{,}106) = \text{max}(995, 3{,}318) = 3{,}318$

**Capital requirement:** $1{,}239 + 3{,}318 = \text{USD} 4{,}557$ million

**Exam trap.** The 95% and 99.9% rows are red herrings. Basel 2.5 fixes the confidence level at 99%, and both terms are added, which is why the charge at least doubled compared with Basel II.

loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
question: The 99% 10-day VaR for an American bank is \$1,000. The average 99% VaR for the recent 60 days is \$480. Over the past seven years, the most stressful 10-day 99% VaR is \$1,100, and the most stressful 60-day average 99% VaR is \$500. The multiplier on the average 99% VaR for the recent 60 days is 3.9, and that of the most stressful average 99% VaR is 3.4. What is the estimated market risk capital charge for this bank under Basel 2.5?
solution:
**Concept**

Basel 2.5 market risk capital adds a stressed VaR charge to the ordinary VaR charge:

max$(\text{VaR}_{t-1}, m_{c} \times\text{VaR}_{\text{avg}}) + \text{max}(\text{sVaR}_{t-1}, m_{s} \times\text{sVaR}_{\text{avg}})$

Each term compares the latest figure with the multiplier times the 60-day average.

**Working**

**VaR term:** max$(1{,}000, 3.9 \times480) = \text{max}(1{,}000, 1{,}872) = 1{,}872$

**Stressed VaR term:** max$(1{,}100, 3.4 \times500) = \text{max}(1{,}100, 1{,}700) = 1{,}700$

**Capital charge:** 1,872 + 1,700 = \$3,572

**Exam trap.** Each multiplier belongs to its own average: 3.9 with the ordinary 60-day average, 3.4 with the stressed 60-day average. In practice the multiplied average almost always exceeds the latest figure, as it does in both terms here.

loText: Describe and calculate the stressed VaR introduced in Basel 2.5 and calculate the market risk capital charge.
question:
A bank is using the VaR and stressed VaR market risk framework in line with the Basel II.5 guidelines. The bank’s internal models for market risk have generated the following risk measures (in USD million) for the current trading book positions:

| Confidence | Latest available 10-day VaR | Latest available 10-day stressed VaR | Average 10-day VaR of previous 60 days | Average 10-day stressed VaR of previous 60 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 95.0% | 289 | 501 | 271 | 572 |
| 99.0% | 513 | 993 | 489 | 1,187 |
| 99.9% | 607 | 1,347 | 564 | 1,412 |

Assuming the supervisory authority has set the multiplication factors for both the VaR and the stressed VaR values to 3, what is the correct capital requirement for general market risk for the bank under Basel II.5?

options.C: USD 4,557 million
options.D: USD 5,028 million

solution:
**Concept**

Basel 2.5 capital for general market risk: max$(\text{VaR}_{t-1}, m_{c} \text{VaR}_{\text{avg}})+\text{max}(\text{sVaR}_{t-1}, m_{s} \text{sVaR}_{\text{avg}})$, using 10-day measures at the 99% confidence level.

**Working**

Use the 99.0% row only.

**VaR term:** max$(513, 3 \times489) = \text{max}(513, 1{,}467) = 1{,}467$

**Stressed VaR term:** max$(993, 3 \times1{,}187) = \text{max}(993, 3{,}561) = 3{,}561$

**Capital requirement:** $1{,}467 + 3{,}561 = \text{USD} 5{,}028$ million

**Exam trap.** The 95% and 99.9% rows are red herrings; the rule fixes the confidence level at 99%. This template is reused with new numbers and the old answer left in as a distractor.

loText: Define in the context of Basel III and calculate where appropriate: - Tier 1 capital and its components - Tier 2 capital and its components - Required Tier 1 equity capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital
question:
A treasury analyst at a bank is calculating the bank’s Basel III regulatory capital ratios for its year-end financial reporting. The analyst considers the following items on the bank’s balance sheet:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Item | Value (EUR millions) |
| Common equity | 2,010 |
| Non-callable preferred equity | 500 |
| Subordinated debt | 1,500 |
| Retained earnings | 3,210 |
| Goodwill from prior acquisitions | 850 |

The bank has total risk-weighted assets of EUR 49,700 million. What is the correct ratio of Core Tier 1 Capital to risk-weighted assets (the CET1 ratio) that the analyst should calculate for the bank?
solution:
**Concept**

Basel III common equity Tier 1 (CET1) is common equity plus retained earnings, less goodwill and other intangibles. Preferred equity is additional Tier 1 and subordinated debt is Tier 2, so neither enters CET1.

**Working**

**CET1 capital:** $2{,}010 + 3{,}210 - 850 = \text{EUR} 4{,}370$ million

**CET1 ratio:** $\frac{4{,}370}{49{,}700} = 8.79\%$

**Exam trap.** Two decisions: what counts as common equity (preferred does not) and what is deducted (goodwill is). The four options are the four combinations.

loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
question:
The CRO of Bank LGX, a non-dividend-paying US-based bank, is preparing a report to the board of directors on the bank’s capital adequacy and planning. Bank LGX is subject to both the Basel framework and the US banking rules governing global systemically important banks (G-SIBs). The bank claims that it was in compliance with all the capital requirements in January 2016 as all Basel III phase-ins have already occurred. The CRO is conducting the analysis for January 2017 using selected and most recent annual performance data:

| Item | Value (USD million), Jan 2017 |
|---|---|
| Common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital | 1,515 |
| Preferred stock (noncumulative) | 100 |
| Tier 2 capital | 827 |
| Risk-weighted assets | 26,395 |
| Total assets | 42,828 |
| Total exposure | 47,460 |

The minimum regulatory capital requirements (including the capital conservation buffer of 2.5% and a G-SIB surcharge of 3.0% of RWA, phased in from January 2016 to January 2019) are:

|  | Jan 2016 | Jan 2017 | Jan 2018 | Jan 2019 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Capital conservation buffer | 0.625% | 1.25% | 1.875% | 2.5% |
| G-SIB surcharge | 0.75% | 1.5% | 2.25% | 3.0% |
| CET1 ratio | 4.5% | 5.25% | 6.5% | 10.0% |
| Tier 1 capital ratio | 6.0% | 6.75% | 8.0% | 11.5% |
| Total capital ratio | 8.0% | 8.75% | 11.5% | 13.5% |
| Leverage ratio | 4.0% | 4.0% | 4.0% | 4.0% |

Given the regulatory benchmarks and the bank’s performance, which of the capital requirements does Bank LGX satisfy as of January 2017?

options.C: Tier 1 capital ratio and Leverage ratio only
options.D: Total capital ratio and CET1 capital ratio only

solution:
**Concept**

Basel III ratios. CET1 ratio = CET1 / RWA. Tier 1 ratio = (CET1 + additional Tier 1) / RWA; noncumulative preferred stock is additional Tier 1. Total capital ratio = (Tier 1 + Tier 2) / RWA. Leverage ratio = Tier 1 / total exposure (not RWA, and not total assets). Compare each with the minimum for the right date.

**Working**

| Ratio | Calculation | Value | Jan 2017 minimum | Met? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CET1 | 1,515/26,395 | 5.74% | 5.25% | Yes |
| Tier 1 | (1,515 + 100)/26,395 | 6.12% | 6.75% | No |
| Total capital | (1,515 + 100 + 827)/26,395 | 9.25% | 8.75% | Yes |
| Leverage | (1,515 + 100)/47,460 | 3.40% | 4.00% | No |

**Exam trap.** The leverage ratio uses total exposure (47,460), which includes off-balance-sheet items, not total assets (42,828). With total assets t […]

loText: Describe the motivations for and calculate the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer, including special rules for globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs).
question: Referring to the Bank LGX capital analysis in the previous question and other considerations for Bank LGX’s capital planning, which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.A: The capital conservation buffer can be met by an increase in Tier 2 capital.
options.B: If the exposure on derivative asset positions decreases, holding other factors constant, the total capital ratio would decrease.
options.C: An increase in the CVA due to the bank’s asset counterparty positions would tend to raise the bank’s risk-weighted assets.
options.D: If the bank raises additional CET1 capital and invests the same amount in gold, Bank LGX’s net stable funding ratio will not change.

solution:
**Concept**

Four separate facts about Basel III. The capital conservation buffer must be met with CET1. Capital ratios have RWA (or exposure) in the denominator. The CVA capital charge adds to RWA. The NSFR compares available stable funding with required stable funding.

**Exam trap.** Option B is a polarity trap on a ratio: a smaller denominator means a larger ratio. Option D looks neutral (“same amount”) but the two sides carry different factors.

**Learning objectives tested:** ORR-22e, ORR-22f.

loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
question: The CRO of a large bank has asked a group of risk managers to prepare a plan to implement the revisions to the Basel III guidelines finalized in December 2017. The bank expects to qualify as a global systemically important bank (G-SIB) by the time the revisions are implemented. Which of the following actions is most appropriate for the bank to take to comply with the revised Basel lll guidelines?

options.A: Introduce an internally created model to determine the bank’s operational risk capital.
options.B: Assign different credit risk weights for residential mortgages based on each mortgage’s loan-to-value ratio.
options.C: Apply the advanced internal rating-based approach for certain types of credit exposures, such as exposures to banks and large corporations.
options.D: Decrease the bank’s target level of its countercyclical buffer and its Basel III Tier 1 leverage ratio.

solution:
**Concept**

December 2017 Basel III reforms. Credit risk standardized approach: more granular risk weights, for example residential mortgages weighted by loan-to-value ratio. IRB: advanced IRB removed for banks, other financial institutions and large corporates. Operational risk: one standardised approach replaces internal models. Leverage ratio: a buffer for G-SIBs. Output floor: 72.5% of standardised RWA.

**Exam trap.** Every wrong option runs against the direction of the reforms, which reduce the role of internal models and tighten requirements.

loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
question:
An operational risk manager is asked to report a bank’s operational risk capital under the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) proposed by the Basel Committee in March 2016. The treasury department produces the following data for the bank, calculated according to the SMA guidelines:

- Business Indicator (BI): EUR 1,200 million
- Internal Loss Multiplier: 1

In addition, the manager uses the Business Indicator buckets in the Business Component presented in the table below:

| **Bucket** | **BI range** | **BI component** |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | EUR 0 to EUR 1 billion | 0.12 × BI |
| 2 | EUR 1 billion to EUR 30 billion | EUR 120 million + 0.15(BI − EUR 1 billion) |
| 3 | Higher than EUR 30 billion | EUR 4.47 billion + 0.18(BI − EUR 30 billion) |

What is the correct operational risk capital that the bank should report under the SMA?

options.C: EUR 158 million
options.D: EUR 180 million

solution:
**Concept**

Under the 2016 standardised measurement approach proposal, capital is the business indicator component times the internal loss multiplier. The component is built from buckets of the business indicator with rising marginal coefficients: the first EUR 1 billion at one rate, the next slice at a higher rate, and so on.

**Working**

The business indicator of EUR 1,200 million falls in the second bucket (EUR 1 billion to EUR 3 billion). **Business indicator component:** $120 + 0.15 \times(1{,}200 - 1{,}000) = 120 + 30 = \text{EUR} 150$ million

**Capital:** $150 \times1 = \text{EUR} 150$ million

**Exam trap.** The coefficients are marginal, like tax brackets: the higher rate applies only to the part of the business indicator inside that bucket.

loText: Explain the elements of the new standardized approach to measure operational risk capital, including the business indicator, internal loss multiplier, and loss component, and calculate the operational risk capital requirement for a bank using this approach.
question:
The following information has been extracted from the P&L of a European bank:

| Year (ended) | 20X6 | 20X7 | 20X8 | 20X9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Interest, leases and dividends | €950m | €1.3bn | €1.8bn | €1.6bn |
| Services | €1.6bn | €2.2bn | €2.6bn | €1.8bn |
| Financial (net P&L on the trading book) | €500m | €1.1bn | €1.3bn | €1.5bn |

Using the Standardized Measurement Approach, the bank’s Business Indicator (BI) for the year ended 31 Dec 20X9 is closest to:

options.C: €3.2 billion
options.D: €500 million

solution:
**Concept**

Under the standardised measurement approach the business indicator (BI) is the sum of three components, each averaged over the latest three years: the interest, leases and dividend component (ILDC), the services component (SC) and the financial component (FC).

**Working**

Use 20X7, 20X8 and 20X9 only.

**ILDC:** $\frac{1.3 + 1.8 + 1.6}{3} = 1.567$ **SC:** $\frac{2.2 + 2.6 + 1.8}{3} = 2.200$ **FC:** $\frac{1.1 + 1.3 + 1.5}{3} = 1.300$

**BI:** $1.567 + 2.200 + 1.300 = \text{EUR} 5.07$ billion

**Exam trap.** Three years, not four. The 20X6 column is a red herring. The business indicator is not the capital charge: capital is the business indicator component (marginal coefficients of 12%, 15% and 18% by bucket) times the internal loss multiplier.
